sections.en:
1 Seth was reported as the inventor of astrology among the Byzantines, cf. Malalas, Chronographia, p. 5 f., ed. Bonn; George the Monk I, p. 10, ed. De Boor; Stephanus the Philosopher in Catalogus, II. 182, v. 26. See also Bouché-Leclercq, Astrologie grecque, p. 578, n. 1, 4. — An excerpt preserved in codex Vindobonensis 1, f. 175 (Catalogus, VI, p. 3) narrates the fable about the angel; cf. Syncellus, Chronographia, p. 16, ed. Bonn and below Glycas p. 140, note 1.
2 Concerning Vettius Valens, Byzantine writers have invented many things. Zonaras XIII, 3 (III, p. 180, Dindorf), Cedrenus I, p. 497, Bonn; Glycas, p. 463 variously narrate that he sought an opportune nativity for the city to be founded by Constantine. But since it is established that Valens flourished under the Antonines (cf. Kroll, Catalogus, II, p. 86), it is an open lie that he presided over the origin of Constantinople, which I would believe was not fabricated before the tenth century. I also found in codex Vaticanus 1065, f. 151, a 'judgment of Valens concerning Muhammad', where similarly they introduce the Greek astrologer conversing with the king of the Persians. — Nevertheless we have found that Constantine consulted certain mathematicians concerning the nativities of new Rome (Preger, Hermes, XXXVI, 339 f.), which at that time was customary to be done even for erecting monuments (cf. Maas, Analecta sacra, Marburg 1901, p. 10) and always prevailed especially concerning royal cities. To Seleucus about to found Seleucia, magi indicated an auspicious or rather inauspicious hour for laying the foundations of the walls (Appian, Syriaca, 57); much later in the same region the Caliph Al-Mansur, assisted by the most famous astrologers of his age, built Baghdad (Suter, Die Mathematiker und Astronomen der Araber, p. 208, 228) and at the time

summary.headline: Divine Providence and Astrological Foundations
summary.text: A theological defense of astrology argues that stars, like nature, the womb, and seed, are not productive causes but act under divine providence. The discussion invokes Abraham, Seth’s angelic instruction, Constantine’s founding of New Rome, and Vettius Valens’s astrological role, with notes on Constantinople, Seleucia, Baghdad, and Byzantine accounts.
